perf.summary: Replace Marshal.AllocHGlobal/FreeHGlobal scratch list with stackalloc; the P/Invoke heap calls defeat Burst and add per-call overhead
perf.currentCost: Two managed P/Invoke transitions (AllocHGlobal + FreeHGlobal) per call. These are managed-runtime calls that Burst cannot compile, forcing the whole method onto the non-Burst path. Also a heap allocation + free on every invocation (latency, fragmentation, no caller pooling).
perf.proposedChange: Since `list` holds values `(byte)i` for i in [0,sigma) and is indexed by byte symbols, sigma is provably <= 256. Use `byte* list = stackalloc byte[256];` (or stackalloc byte[sigma] if Burst allows variable-length; fixed 256 is safest/blittable) and drop both Marshal calls. The list never escapes the function.
perf.rationale: stackalloc is a single stack-pointer bump (effectively free) versus a heap alloc/free pair, and it keeps the method Burst-compilable and branch/exception-free. 256 bytes on the stack is trivial and fully within one cache line set, improving locality vs. a fresh heap block.
perf.risk: sigma must be <= 256 (guaranteed: list values are byte and inputs index it as byte, so any sigma>256 is already semantically broken/truncating in current code). Using a fixed 256 wastes a few bytes when sigma is smaller but is fully safe and avoids variable-length-stackalloc concerns under Burst.

perf.summary: Replace the byte-at-a-time backward shift loop with a single overlapping memmove (Buffer.MemoryCopy)
perf.currentCost: `for (int j = pos; j > 0; j--) list[j] = list[j-1];` is `pos` dependent load/store iterations with a per-byte loop branch and a serial dependency chain; for large alphabets and high positions this dominates.
perf.proposedChange: Shift `list[0..pos-1]` up by one with a single overlapping move: `Buffer.MemoryCopy(list, list + 1, sigma - 1, pos);` then `list[0] = symbol;`. (Direction is high-to-low / non-overlapping-destructive but MemoryCopy handles overlap correctly for dst>src copying low->... use the overlap-safe move semantics.)
perf.rationale: Collapses `pos` scalar iterations into one bulk move the JIT/Burst can vectorize, removing the per-element loop branch and shortening the dependency chain. For typical MTF where recently-used symbols cluster near front pos is small, but the worst case (cold symbols, pos~sigma) becomes a single SIMD-friendly copy.
perf.risk: Buffer.MemoryCopy is a managed BCL method and may not be Burst-intrinsic; under Burst prefer UnsafeUtility.MemMove. Overlap direction must be handled (dst = src+1 overlapping forward); use a guaranteed overlap-safe memmove, not memcpy. If neither memmove intrinsic is available under Burst, keep the scalar loop. Net: only apply if an overlap-safe, Burst-friendly move primitive exists in the project.

perf.summary: Inconsistent AggressiveInlining: Encode is marked, Decode is not, and neither is a hot leaf
perf.currentCost: Encode carries [MethodImpl(AggressiveInlining)] but is a multi-loop, allocation-bearing method — inlining it bloats the caller with no benefit and is asymmetric with Decode which has no attribute. Inconsistent API surface.
perf.proposedChange: Either remove AggressiveInlining from Encode (it is not a small leaf), or add it to Decode for symmetry. Recommended: remove from both; let the compiler decide for these larger routines.
perf.rationale: Inlining large bodies increases instruction-cache pressure at every call site without speeding the inner loops (the cost is in the O(len*sigma) loops, not call overhead). Consistency aids discoverability and avoids surprising codegen.
perf.risk: None semantically; purely codegen-size/consistency. Verify no caller relies on inlining for a measured win (unlikely given the body size).

perf.summary: List-initialization loop is loop-invariant per call and the linear search rescans from 0 each symbol; both are inherent O(sigma) but the init can use a fill primitive
perf.currentCost: `for (i=0;i<sigma;i++) list[i]=(byte)i;` is a scalar identity fill each call. The encode search `while (list[pos]!=input[i]) pos++;` is an unavoidable O(pos) probe but the cast `(byte)pos` and reload of input[i] in the shift epilogue are minor redundancies.
perf.proposedChange: Hoist `byte sym = input[i];` once per outer iteration and reuse it for the compare, output, and `list[0]=sym` (avoids reloading input[i] after pointer-aliasing the compiler may not prove non-aliased with output). The identity-fill is fundamental; leave as-is or keep scalar (Burst vectorizes the simple `(byte)i` pattern poorly anyway).
perf.rationale: Caching `input[i]` in a local removes a potential reload that the compiler cannot elide because `output` and `input` are unrelated pointers it must assume may alias `list` writes; the local breaks that conservative reload.
perf.risk: None — `input[i]` does not change within the iteration (input and list/output are distinct buffers by contract). Purely removes a redundant load.
